cases.title: Nenskra hydropower: about 700 hectares granted in Chuberi and Nakra, and pasture compensation left unpaid
cases.place: Chuberi and Nakra valleys, Mestia Municipality, Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti, Georgia
cases.point: Mestia Municipality centre point (GeoNames entry 7667559, 43.06058 N, 42.48126 E). The Chuberi and Nakra valleys lie in the west of the municipality; no source I opened gave coordinates for Chuberi village.

lenders.name: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)
lenders.role: Two sources give different roles and neither explains the other. The EIB Complaints Mechanism report of 7 February 2020 says the project company JSC Nenskra Hydro was 85% owned by Korea Water Resources Corporation, 10% by JSC Partnership Fund and 5% by the EBRD. The Early Warning System project record for EBRD-46778 lists a loan of USD 214 million with a board date of 31 January 2018, status 'Approved', and no equity. EBRD management later told its own accountability office that the project had been cancelled.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: Approved financing of up to USD 150 million on 6 February 2018. The Complaints Mechanism report of 7 February 2020 lists the project status as 'Pending signature'.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank (ADB)
lenders.role: The Early Warning System record for ADB-49223-001 lists a proposed ADB loan of USD 214 million and a USD 100 million B-loan for which ADB is lender of record, USD 314 million in total. The record was disclosed on 21 March 2017 and lists the project as 'Proposed'.

lenders.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)
lenders.role: Listed as a financing institution on the Early Warning System record for the project (AIIB-000032). No amount or date is given there. A November 2017 footnote in the EIB report lists ADB, EBRD, EIB, KDB, AIIB and K-sure as potential lenders and does not say which finally took part.

companies.name: Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-water)
companies.role: Majority owner of the project company JSC Nenskra Hydro. The EIB Complaints Mechanism (2020) puts its share at 85%; OC Media (2018) puts it at 80%. K-water is itself 91.5% owned by the South Korean government and 8.5% by the Korea Development Bank, per the Early Warning System record.

companies.name: Salini Impregilo
companies.role: Listed as the project contractor on the Early Warning System records. A contractor on its own is not an outside-money link; it is listed here because the records name it.

companies.name: JSC Partnership Fund
companies.role: Georgian state investment fund and part-owner of JSC Nenskra Hydro: 10% per the EIB Complaints Mechanism (2020), 20% per OC Media (2018).

cases.community: CEE Bankwatch Network visited the Nenskra and Nakra valleys twice in July 2017 and interviewed 20 households. Its report says that "In total almost 700 hectares of mostly forested land were granted to the project promoter", made up of 96.2 hectares granted in Chuberi for USD 1 and 600.0252 hectares granted "to use for 55 years"; the report does not say where the second block lies. The company's Land Acquisition and Livelihood Restoration Plan lists 80 households, 363 people, as affected; the areas Bankwatch surveyed account for 47 of those households and 212 people, being 9 households at the dam and reservoir, 11 at the construction camp and 27 at the Nakra weir and transfer tunnel intake. The plan says the people affected are "mainly affected by the temporary or permanent loss of pastures for their animals", and names the pastures Kvemo Memuli, Mashrichala, Lagiri and Khurkhtsari. It carries a budget line for "compensating 36ha of land belonging to 61 households". People losing pastures were offered either 20 tonnes of hay or 20,000 GEL a year for up to seven years, and Bankwatch found that where a pasture was shared the offer went to only one user. A female-headed household in Sgurishi was offered nothing: "no compensation was offered for the temporary loss of the pasture area in Kvemo Memuli". Compensation for cabins ranged from 5,000 to 16,000 GEL, and where a cabin was co-used "4 to 5 households would have to share compensation of 8000 GEL", under 2,000 GEL each. Two wooden cabins on the left bank of the Nakra river were not recorded at all. Access to cabins is lost "either temporarily, for seven years during construction, or permanently". Agreements were due in April 2017 for Nenskra and August 2017 for Nakra: "This has not happened, but it is unclear what the new timeline is." Bankwatch found no compensation had been paid. The Nenskra valley has 1,148 residents in 268 households and the Nakra valley 300 residents in 85 households, most of them Svan, per the EIB report. OC Media reported in 2018 that construction launched in 2015 and that Green Alternative put the land to be flooded at up to 267 hectares of forest and communal land.
cases.displaced_note: No physical resettlement is recorded in anything I opened. The 80 households and 363 people are the company's own count of people affected by land acquisition and economic displacement, not people moved from homes.
cases.suppression: Bankwatch's 2017 report says "several respondents feared repercussions" for speaking out. Its October 2017 blog describes a developer meeting in Chuberi where opponents "marched out as a sign of protest" after their questions went unanswered, and says one resident was told she was asking one too many questions. OC Media reported dozens protesting in Chuberi, with a photo caption dated 21 April 2018. The requesters who went to the EBRD's accountability office asked for their identities to be kept confidential.
cases.outcome: The EBRD's accountability office registered the request on 11 June 2018, completed its eligibility assessment on 1 October 2018, and issued a compliance review report, the requesters' comments and a Management Action Plan on 10 August 2020, followed by a monitoring plan on 30 November 2020 and seven monitoring reports between 22 April 2021 and 1 May 2024. The case page says a Management Action Plan was issued "to address the non-compliance" but does not summarise the findings. Management then told the office that the project had been cancelled and that the remaining open actions were project-specific; the office closed the case conditionally on 24 June 2026, saying the obligations should be reactivated if the project is revived, materially restructured or resubmitted to the EBRD Board. The EIB Complaints Mechanism, reporting on 7 February 2020, found that there was "no evidence that the Bank took the adequate steps to assure itself of the proper application of Standard 7" on indigenous peoples, that the vulnerability test used to exclude the Svans was erroneous because it relied on relative poverty, that the labour influx assessment was "insufficient at this time", that it could not verify compliance on alternatives, and that the EIB "underestimated social challenges associated with the project".

cases.confidence_note: What is firmly recorded is the land transfer and the compensation offers. The grant of about 700 hectares, the pasture and cabin offers, the household left with no offer at Kvemo Memuli and the unmet April and August 2017 deadlines all come from CEE Bankwatch Network's field report of 11 September 2017, which rests on two visits and 20 household interviews and on the company's own land plan. The dam itself was never built and the project was cancelled, so the flooding of 267 hectares and the loss of pastures during a seven-year construction period did not happen as planned; the land grant and the unpaid or inadequate offers did. The EIB Complaints Mechanism report of 7 February 2020 assesses the Bank's work up to loan approval and records no completed land take, no tree felling and no income loss; that is an absence in a bank-focused document, not a denial. The two ownership figures for K-water, 85% and 80%, and the two accounts of the EBRD's role, 5% equity and a USD 214 million loan, are given above as each source states them. No source I read reconciles either pair.
cx: Residents of Chuberi, Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti, supported by CEE Bankwatch Network and Green Alternative
cases.ecosystem: The scheme would have put a 125 metre dam on the Nenskra river with a reservoir of about 3 square kilometres, and diverted the Nakra river through a 12 kilometre transfer tunnel. Green Alternative told OC Media the diversion would leave about 10 per cent of the Nakra's average annual flow downstream and that up to 267 hectares of forest and communal land would be flooded. The Bern Convention Standing Committee re-examined a complaint in April 2020 about the threat to Svaneti 1, a candidate Emerald site. The reservoir was never built.

lvwhy.project: The land grants and the compensation plan existed only because the hydropower scheme was being prepared for international lenders.
lvwhy.land: About 700 hectares of mostly forested land, including 96.2 hectares in Chuberi granted for USD 1, were transferred to the project company, and summer pastures and cabins used by households were covered by the land plan.
lvwhy.finance: The land plan was issued, in Bankwatch's words, to comply with the financing requirements of European and Asian multilateral development institutions.

cases.title: Mzuzu water project: cracked houses and unpaid land compensation at Kazando, Chipambo and Geisha
cases.place: Kazando, Chipambo and Geisha, Mzuzu area, Northern Region, Malawi
cases.point: Mzuzu city (approximate). The reports name the three communities but give no coordinates for them; the project serves Mzuzu and Ekwendeni.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: The Board of Directors approved up to EUR 24.6 million in November 2016 and the finance contract was signed on 4 July 2017. Total estimated project cost EUR 60.4 million. The promoter is the Northern Region Water Board (EIB Complaints Mechanism reports, 2022 and 2024).

cases.community: Members of several communities in the Mzuzu area complained to the EIB's Complaints Mechanism on 9 July 2021 about property damage during construction and about no assessment report or compensation list being released. The office ran three parallel processes. For Chipambo and Geisha, its final monitoring report of 15 December 2022 records that 234 households were assessed for land valuations, that 231 signed their valuations on 6 July 2022, that two were invited to sign later and that one refused; the Regional Commissioner for Lands North sent the final valuation report to the promoter on 11 July 2022, and the promoter paid 219 members between 26 August and 21 September 2022, with 15 notified to collect and nine members of the grievance committee not collecting. On damage to houses, the promoter assessed the damage between 23 September and 3 October 2022 and disclosed the results on 19 October 2022; on 13 December 2022, 20 of 38 affected members were paid. Eleven objected because, in the report's words, "some of cracks were not included in the assessment of the damage", and the omitted cracks were assessed the same day. Three were unavailable, three said they would hire a private valuer, and one household refused payment because, the report says, "his house collapsed". For Kazando, the settlement of 5 July 2022 covered payment of remaining compensation to 13 households, a damage assessment and payment, three communal water points, road maintenance and the rehabilitation of a hall as a health centre; the draft valuation covered 14 missing households and was signed on 8 July 2022, the damage assessment was completed by 13 July 2022 and disclosed to 17 households, 17 affected members were paid on 4 August 2022 and 15 households were paid for damaged structures on 26 August 2022. The office's second monitoring report says the household counts of 13, 14, 15 and 17 differ across its own sections and does not reconcile them, and it does not give the amounts paid. A separate strand of the complaint, from one owner who said the works cracked his house, was settled on 3 May 2022 after the owner and the promoter jointly chose an independent engineer, who found it "cannot be established" that the excavation works caused the damage; both parties accepted that.
cases.displaced_note: No resettlement or physical displacement is recorded. The payments concern land valuations and damage to standing houses.
cases.outcome: At Kazando three communal water points were installed by March 2023 and the promoter said 22 new households had been connected to the supply by December 2023; grading of the main road and smaller roads was finished by February 2023. Three actions were still open at 6 March 2024: three further communal water points requested in December 2023, with one expected by the end of June 2024, and the cost and the work of rehabilitating the health centre, which the promoter estimated at MWK 47 million at the end of 2023 and which the promoter and the community were still trying to fund. The Chipambo and Geisha monitoring phase ended in December 2022, with the office treating the damage point as closed because most affected members had been paid and the promoter's offer and grievance process remained open. The case page still lists monitoring as open. A separate complaint on the same project, SG/E/2024/07, was brought by an instrumentation engineer whose work was used in a dam safety inception report without a contract or payment; the parties agreed a contract and payment and the office closed it on 21 June 2024. That one is a contract dispute, not community harm.

cases.title: Nis railway bypass: a block of flats marked for demolition, six families bought out and an eviction petition
cases.point: Nis city centre (approximate). The Complaints Mechanism gives no street or settlement name for the building.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: The Board of Directors approved an investment loan of up to EUR 134 million on 1 December 2017 and a further EUR 100 million in July 2024. The borrower is the Republic of Serbia and the promoter is Serbian Railways Infrastructure.

lenders.name: Western Balkans Investment Framework
lenders.role: EUR 106 million in grants, per the Complaints Mechanism's reports of 5 November 2025 and 10 March 2026.

cases.conditions: The City of Nis and the promoter adopted a Resettlement Action Plan in October 2019. For the five remaining tenant families it set out tenant-purchase of their flats followed by entry into the expropriation procedure. The Complaints Mechanism records that "The arrangement foreseen in the RAP was not implemented."

companies.name: MIN Holding (Masinska industrija Nis)
companies.role: Owner of the residential building marked for demolition; a limited liability company that went bankrupt in 2015. It filed the eviction petition against the complainant.

cases.community: A resident of Nis complained to the EIB's Complaints Mechanism on 8 September 2022. The office's dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 says: "The residential building in which the complainant lives is set to be demolished in order to complete the project." The building has 16 units. Five were unoccupied. Of the 11 rented to former employees of MIN Holding, six families regularised their status, became owners, received compensation and moved out. Five families, including the complainant, remained tenants. The City of Nis offered social housing, which the complainant rejected because the unit was smaller and the tenancy ran five years with possible extension while the existing tenancy was indefinite. The report states: "MIN Holding filed an eviction petition against the complainant in September 2022." In October 2022 the complainant petitioned the court for the right to tenant-purchase the flat. A second complaint, SG/E/2025/13, was received on 24 September 2025 from an employee of the promoter who lives with his wife and three children in a flat the promoter owns on the Stanicenje-Dimitrovgrad section; the initial assessment report of 10 March 2026 says the flat "will need to be demolished" and records no demolition, eviction or rehousing yet.
cases.displaced_label: families who moved out of the building after being made owners and compensated
cases.displaced_note: The dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 says six of the 11 tenant families "regularised their status, became owners, received compensation and moved out". It does not give the dates or the amounts. What the five remaining tenant families received is covered by the confidential settlement of September 2025.
cases.outcome: Dialogue ran from December 2022 to September 2025, with two joint sessions in May and December 2023 and many bilateral meetings, involving the City of Nis, MIN Holding's bankruptcy administrator and the Serbian Bankruptcy Supervision Agency. The parties signed a final settlement in September 2025 and agreed to keep its content confidential. In January 2026 the promoter and the complainant confirmed the agreement was "fully implemented" and the Complaints Mechanism ended monitoring on 16 January 2026. The office lists the outcome as a friendly solution with no suggestions for improvement. It notes that legal complexity, parallel court proceedings, elections, leadership changes and the fatal accident at Novi Sad railway station, which led to nationwide protests, delayed the process. The second complaint on the Stanicenje-Dimitrovgrad section is in collaborative dispute resolution.

cases.title: Tunis suburban railway: half a property taken at Bardo in 2014, with compensation still in court
cases.point: Bardo square, Tunis (approximate). The conclusions report places the property "in front of the Bardo square" and gives no street address.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: The Board of Directors approved a loan of up to EUR 177 million on 21 October 2009 and the finance contract was signed on 10 December 2010. The promoter is Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide (RFR), a special purpose company set up by the Tunisian government.

lenders.name: Agence Francaise de Developpement (AFD)
lenders.role: Co-financier and, in the conclusions report's words, the leading institution. The report gives no amount.

lenders.name: KfW
lenders.role: Co-financier. The report gives no amount.

lenders.name: European Commission, Neighbourhood Investment Facility (NIF)
lenders.role: Co-financier. The report gives no amount.

cases.conditions: The EIB decided in 2013 to waive the requirement for a satisfactory Resettlement Action Plan before first disbursement. The Complaints Mechanism treated that waiver as within the discretion of the Bank's governing bodies, but found the Bank breached its own standards by not pausing negotiations until it had received a satisfactory resettlement plan or framework.
cases.community: The complainant is described by the office as "a local resident whose property located in front of the Bardo square had been partially expropriated". The report says "only half of the complainant's land was expropriated", under an expropriation decree dated 7 January 2014, and that he said the remainder was no longer suitable for construction. A Court of First Instance judgment of 26 June 2014 dismissed the Public Prosecutor's demand to take possession, treating the case as invalid because "the first of the defendants was deceased". The complainant said the compensation offered was "1/8th of the real value". The promoter said its first offer was "250 dinars/m2" and that after a refusal it was raised to "400 dinars/m2", after which the file went to court; the promoter told the EIB it had no information to share on the compensation proceeding. A further Court of First Instance decision of 23 October 2017 is referenced. The promoter refused in April 2016 to buy the remaining part. On the wider expropriation, the report records that in September 2016 "out of 31 expropriation procedures on line D, only three were in process of being executed"; that in March 2015 there were 95 pending files, of which 69 "would refer to land that is not in use at all"; and that in November 2018 there were "29 cases for Line D still awaiting a judgment". It attributes delays to judicial workload, unclear transitional provisions after the 2016 expropriation law, and inheritance problems. In March 2019 the Bardo municipal council unanimously decided on "the temporary stop of the RFR works in Bardo".
cases.displaced_note: No household is recorded as having been moved from a home. The documented loss is land: half of one property taken under the 2014 decree, with the remainder said to be unbuildable.
cases.outcome: The office found the expropriation allegation ungrounded in terms of the EIB's obligations, and found the allegations about refusing to take the whole property or to compensate in kind ungrounded. It found the public consultation allegation grounded, citing a "significant gap between national EIA law and EIB standards" and a lack of engagement with civil society and the public. It said the valuation had not been indexed, that the project "may have a negative impact on the complainant's right on the expropriated land", and that the 2014 compensation was likely to be inadequate "if not addressed through a process of recalculation". On the Tunisian system it noted that "the compensation amounts offered are very low and it is often necessary to go to court". It recommended that EIB services document the gap between the 2014 amount and current indexed market prices within six months and agree how to bridge it, that they support a Stakeholder Engagement Plan covering Bardo residents and businesses, and that they support the promoter's social reporting, possibly through a technical assistance team at the promoter's headquarters. EIB services were to report to the Management Committee in 2020 with implementation monitored by the end of the first quarter of 2021. The case page records monitoring closed on 31 December 2024.

cases.confidence_note: The expropriation decree of 7 January 2014, the two court dates, the two offers of 250 and 400 dinars per square metre and the office's view that the 2014 amount is likely inadequate without recalculation all come from the lender's own conclusions report. What was finally paid is not public. The documented loss is one household's; the figures of 31, 95 and 29 are counts of expropriation files on line D, not of people, and the report gives no total of households expropriated for the project. I read the conclusions report through about 100,000 of its 112,012 characters; the text available to me cut off part way through its discussion of the lack of indexation, so I did not read its closing paragraphs and do not claim what they say. Lead 24 bundled several Tunisian road and rail complaints. The Sfax interchanges are already on the map as sfax-rocade-interchanges and were not re-researched. cases.title: Bogota Metro Line 1: 1,264 buildings demolished along the route
cases.place: First Line of the Bogota Metro, Bosa to Calle 72, Bogota, Colombia
cases.point: Avenida Caracas at Calle 26, a point on the Line 1 alignment (approximate). The demolitions run the length of the 24 km route through Bosa, Kennedy, Puente Aranda, Los Martires, Antonio Narino, Santa Fe, Chapinero, Teusaquillo and Barrios Unidos.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: A framework loan for Bogota Sustainable Transport of up to USD 480 million was approved on 17 July 2018. Tranche 1, USD 56 million for Metro Line 1, was signed on 6 August 2018 and is recorded as fully disbursed; tranche 2, USD 50 million for Metro Line 2, was signed on 8 May 2023. The same report also says the EIB approved the financing of Metro Line 1 on 5 February 2025.

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Named as a co-financier of Metro Line 1 by the EIB Complaints Mechanism's initial assessment report of 19 November 2025. No amount is given there. The IDB's Environmental and Social Grievance Protocol was handling a separate grievance from the same complainant.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Named as a co-financier of Metro Line 1 by the same report. No amount is given there. The World Bank Inspection Panel was notified of the complaint.

cases.conditions: Property acquisition and relocation were carried out under the project's Resettlement Plan, adopted as Resolucion 189 de 2018 by the Empresa Metro de Bogota. The EIB complaint turns on whether shopkeepers along Calle 72 who were not expropriated should have been covered by that plan.

companies.name: Metro Linea 1 S.A.S (ML1)
companies.role: Concessionaire responsible for the design, construction, operation and maintenance of Metro Line 1, per the EIB Complaints Mechanism (2025). Its owners are not named in any document I opened, so no headquarters is given here.

cases.community: The Bogota city government published figures on 29 March 2023, current to 28 February 2023. The acquisition target for Line 1 was 1,427 properties; 1,373 had been handed over and 54 were outstanding, which the Empresa Metro de Bogota put at 96.3 per cent. The city wrote: "se han demolido 1.264 construcciones a lo largo del trazado, cercanas al 89% del total" - 1,264 buildings demolished along the route, about 89 per cent of the total. 1,046 properties had been passed to the concessionaire. Of the 54 still outstanding, 19 had a promise of sale or an expropriation resolution, 24 were in notification and acceptance of an offer, and 11 were in the offer process. The manager of the Empresa Metro de Bogota, Leonidas Narvaez, said the acquisition "nos ha significado una inversion a pesos corrientes de 1,05 billones de pesos" - about 1.05 trillion current pesos, including social compensation. The city says social compensation was paid to people who had to relocate under the Resettlement Plan but gives no number of households or businesses. Separately, a shop owner on Calle 72 complained to the EIB's Complaints Mechanism; its initial assessment report of 19 November 2025 records his account that road closures and congestion since May 2024 had cut customer access, reduced sales and profit, raised the risk of insolvency and led to staff dismissals, and that the project excluded "project-affected business owners along Calle 72 and adjacent areas" from the Resettlement Action Plan. The office recorded these as allegations, made no findings, and decided to carry out a compliance review.
cases.displaced_note: The city's figures count properties and demolished buildings, not households or businesses. The city says social compensation was paid to people who had to relocate but publishes no count of them in the article I read, so no displaced figure is given here.
cases.outcome: The Inspectorate General referred the shopkeeper's complaint to the Complaints Mechanism on 31 December 2024. It was declared admissible on 14 February 2025 and registration was notified on 27 February 2025. Virtual calls with the complainant, the promoter and the concessionaire ran from March to July 2025. Both sides first showed interest in dispute resolution but disagreed on its scope, and one side then preferred a compliance review, so dispute resolution was dropped. The office will run a compliance review covering environmental and social impact assessment, involuntary resettlement and stakeholder engagement, coordinating with the IDB and the World Bank Inspection Panel. On 17 September 2025 the city said more than USD 1,480 million of lender funds, which it put at about 5.7 billion pesos, were approved and due to be disbursed before January 2026; it did not break the figure down by lender and did not mention the EIB.

They count buildings and properties, not people, so the number displaced is not known from them. dropped.reason: Harm not documented anywhere I could open. The EBRD's accountability office took the case for problem-solving only, and its case page (https://www.ebrd.com/work-with-us/projects/ipam/2020/07.html, opened) says the problem-solving ended with no agreement reached on 7 September 2022 and lists no finding; the allegation that mining took grazing lands so residents can no longer rely on livestock breeding is the 372 requesters' own account. The office never tested it, and the requesters asked for confidentiality for fear of retaliation, so there are no named places or figures to check. The Early Warning System record (https://ewsdata.rightsindevelopment.org/projects/EBRD-49041/, opened) gives the EBRD loan as USD 40 million with a board date of 29 November 2017 for Tumad Madencilik's Lapseki and Ivrindi mines, and records no impacts, no land acquisition and no complaint; it lists a Livelihood Restoration Framework without summarising it. A Turkish-language search for grazing land loss at Degirmenbasi returned only the EBRD's own 2017 financing announcement, Hurriyet Daily News and Anadolu Agency coverage of the loan, and a Nurol annual report page, none of them about the village's pastures. With the office silent and no court, audit, study, press or field research on the pasture loss, test 2 fails.

The EIB side records only expected damage, so I have not written it, and the ADB records for the same project sit in another agent's batch. I opened the case page (https://www.eib.org/en/about/accountability/complaints/cases/greater-colombo-wastewater-project-sg-e-2024-27) and the dispute resolution report of 30 June 2025 (https://www.eib.org/files/complaints/2025-06-30PUBLIC-Disputeresolutionreport-SG-E-2024-27GreaterColomboWastewaterProject.pdf). The 37 households of Narahenpita feared that trenching and excavation beside the Narahenpita pumping station "may cause damage to the surrounding houses" and "may cause land subsidence in the vicinity of the construction site", and that the station "may cause unpleasant smells, mosquito infestation and other potential health risks". The report records no actual damage to any house and no odour yet, and says construction has generally progressed peacefully since October 2024. The friendly solution entitles 23 first-row owners to a package of 12 months' rent and transport costs and says second-row residents will be relocated only if structural stability is at risk, with minor damage repaired in place; all of that is forward-looking and the report does not record anyone having moved. EIB financing is EUR 50 million approved on 19 May 2016 and signed on 20 January 2017, borrower the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka, promoter the Colombo Municipal Council. If the ADB complaint or the Sri Lankan Auditor General's report on the programme records damage that actually happened, the case belongs to whoever holds those records, as one case naming the EIB too.

Only potential harm, and no harm of any kind recorded. I opened the case page for SG/E/2020/20 (https://www.eib.org/de/about/accountability/complaints/cases/lebanon-round-1-wind-project-i-sg-e-2020-20?lang=en). The allegations are "potential environmental and social risks and impacts": the site lying within a nature reserve, a tourist site and a bird migration route, water resource vulnerabilities, potential noise pollution, and doubts about the promoters' capacity to implement the project. The page records no land lost, no household affected and no finding, and gives no EIB loan amount or promoter name. Test 2 fails on predicted harm. A later case on the same project, SG/INA/2026/07, is listed on the EIB site but I did not open it.

The link test fails, and the office's own report says so. I read the conclusions report annexed to the final reply (http://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2010-08-ecocimento-fibre-cement-moz-annex-1-public.pdf), about 11 numbered pages, in full. Section 5.1 states: "The Maputo site was not part of the Ecocimento Fiber Cement Project financed by the Bank." Section 2.3 adds that the Maputo decontamination was dropped from the final project description, which covered only Dondo. The EIB-CM found that an outdated project description naming Maputo was left on the EIB website by error and that the borrower used it to mislead the complainant. The EIB's loan was EUR 1.3 million from the Cotonou Investment Facility, for the Dondo plant. On the asbestos site itself there is documented health harm: a consulting occupational hygienist's report of 24 November 2008 found friable asbestos "putting the workers and residents' health at risk"; a MICOA letter of 28 July 2010 described exposed fibres as "constituting a danger to the health of the local inhabitants"; and a MICOA audit of 27 July 2009 found a risk of contamination for public health. But no outside lender, financier or foreign owner is documented for the Maputo site. The borrower's voting shares were held 95% by Lusalite de Mozambique S.a.r.l. and 2.5% each by two named individuals, and the Mozambican state holds 20% of Lusalite; the report does not state Lusalite's nationality, so I cannot call it a foreign owner. Banco Comercial e de Investimentos SARL co-financed the project and gave Ecocimento a line of credit, but the report does not connect it to the Maputo site, and a domestic bank would not pass in any case. A national court injunction ordered the seller of the site to clean up the asbestos; the defendant's name is redacted in the report.

Timing fails and no harm is recorded. The project was cancelled on 4 November 2011 and the EBRD's compliance review then found nothing. I opened the EBRD PCM annual report for 2011 (https://www.ebrd.com/downloads/integrity/pcm_annual_report_2011.pdf), which records four complaints received in March 2011: one from Green Alternative on the adequacy of the environmental and social appraisal, two from David Chipashvili for project-affected persons, and one from Nino Saginashvili, a resident of the Avchala district. Twelve Avchala families raised concerns that the railway would "transport hazardous materials through their densely populated community", along with safety, health, declining property values, water supply and visual impacts, and "the decisions regarding who is compensated and resettled and who is not". Those are stated concerns, not recorded harm. The report says: "Unfortunately, on 4 November the Project was cancelled", and the problem-solving initiative was terminated on 7 November 2011. I then opened the EBRD annual report for 2012 (https://www.ebrd.com/downloads/integrity/annual_report_2012.pdf), which says "No findings of non-compliance were made following the Compliance Review process", posted 23 July 2012, and records no land acquisition, house purchase, resettlement or compensation at Avchala before cancellation. I also opened Bankwatch's project page (https://bankwatch.org/project-relationship/tbilisi-railway-bypass-project-georgia), which carries the 2011 complaint and the financing but nothing on Avchala. Both EBRD URLs returned the documents normally; neither was blocked. The main session reports that the map's own complaint register holds no ipam:2011/01-04 record, its EBRD coverage starting at ipam:2015/03, so the lead's key cannot be confirmed either.

lead_notes.note: Accounted for inside the case mzuzu-nrwb-water-efficiency-house-damage, which is the kept entry for lead 22. Noting here only that the second complaint on the same project, SG/E/2024/07 (conclusions report opened at https://www.eib.org/files/complaints/20240621PUBLICConclusionsReportSGE202407Malawi.pdf), is an unpaid consultant's contract dispute over the Lunyangwa dam safety management plan and not community harm, so it is not the basis of the case. Lead 22 itself is kept as a case, not dropped.

One case written from this lead, rfr-bardo-expropriation-tunis, on the Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide complaint SG/E/2016/04, where the office records an expropriation decree of 7 January 2014 taking half a property at Bardo and compensation still in court. The Sfax interchanges part of the lead is already on the map as sfax-rocade-interchanges and was not re-researched. The other five stretches are drops, with the pages I opened: S4 Deviation Zarzis, conclusions report of 19 October 2023 (http://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2021-23-mrii-s4-zarzis-rapport-de-conclusions-final-public.pdf) - land acquisition had not started, "l'acquisition et l'indemnisation des terrains n'ayant pas encore debute", no compensation paid, no demolition carried out, and the 565 plots, 1,402 people and 6 houses are planned impacts from the 2018 resettlement plan; the office found only that compensation "pourrait bien etre significativement inferieures a la valeur de marche", which is a likelihood, so test 2 and test 3 both fail. Autoroute du Centre SG/E/2025/01 (https://www.eib.org/fr/about/accountability/complaints/cases/autoroute-du-centre-sg-e-2025-01?lang=de) - allegations of potential flood risk and houses close to the highway, dialogue ongoing, no findings. G1 Penetrante Sud SG/E/2022/20 (https://www.eib.org/en/about/accountability/complaints/cases/g1-penetrante-sud-sg-e-2022-20?lang=en) - a verbal expropriation request and a compensation offer the complainant thought too low; he went to national court, got a revised offer, told the office he was satisfied, and the case closed with no recommendations; a compensation dispute settled upward is not documented harm. X4, part of Modernisation Routiere II, SG/E/2024/22, dispute resolution report of 9 April 2025 (https://www.eib.org/files/complaints/2025-04-09PUBLICRapportderesolutiondesdifferendsSG-E-2024-22ModernisationRoutiereIIX4.pdf) - residents of an informal neighbourhood near the new road raised cracks in house walls, blocked runoff and a degraded track, the promoter considered it unlikely the works caused the cracks, and the office made no finding on causation and left the cracks to a judicial expert or the regional conciliation commission. Autoroute Sfax-Gabes SG/E/2012/01 (https://www.eib.org/en/about/accountability/complaints/cases/sg-e-2012-01-autoroute-sfax-gabes) - the complainant alleged his land was expropriated with no compensation offer and that he was threatened by the promoter's employees; the office found no EIB maladministration, noted the case was before the national courts, and closed it with "no grounds", and no document on the page records what happened to the land or the man.
